name: The Four-Trunked Survivor

location.address: On the Vestingen (Ieper fortifications) walking route, on the slope beside the Menin Gate, Ieper, Belgium

access: Free. Stands in the open, on the public Vestingen (fortifications) walking park that rings Ieper, beside the Menin Gate; the City of Ieper itself runs a public audio-guide stop here (Dutch and English) as part of its heritage walking route, no ticket or permission needed.
transport: Ieper railway station, roughly a 15-minute walk east via the town centre and Menin Gate.
verify_notes: DEEPENS: Ypres (would be ypr_005; Ypres currently has 4 published trees, ypr_001-004, all within a few km of Ieper centre but none at this location). Hard rule 10 checked: genuinely public, no permission needed, not private land -- it sits on the city's own Vestingen fortifications park, part of a signposted heritage walking route with an official city audio guide ('De Boom Vertelt' / 'The tree speaks'), open ground, free. Species/planting: a sweet chestnut planted 'rond 1860' (city's own words) when the military fortress was converted into a public promenade park; that gives roughly 160-166 years depending on exact planting year, none of the sources give a more precise date, so treat 'roughly 165 years' as a loose figure rather than a precise one. Girth 9.10 m (910 cm) is the TRUNK BASE circumference of the whole four-stemmed structure, not a single-trunk measurement -- it is a fused multi-stem base, so the writer should not repeat 910 cm as an ordinary single-trunk girth without saying so. History: the original single trunk was reduced to a stump during WWI shelling (Ypres was flattened 1914-18) but the root system survived and four new trunks grew from it after the armistice; all four survived WWII despite widespread wartime felling for firewood in Ieper, reportedly spared specifically because the tree stands on a slope and felling it risked dropping trunks onto nearby houses (per the city's own account). Contest says it is one of only two Ieper trees to have lived through both world wars (the other reportedly a three-stemmed hazel on the ramparts, not independently checked here, not a candidate in this brief). Won Belgian 'Tree of the Year 2020' (Baillet Latour prize) and placed 12th at the 2021 European final with 30,886 votes. Coordinate is the contest's own GPS listing (N50 51 8.74, E2 53 26.26), which converts exactly to 50.852428, 2.890628 and sits about 170-175 m from the Menin Gate itself, consistent with 'on the fortifications beside the Menin Gate, on a slope.' Could not independently pin it via OSM tree nodes (Overpass API returned HTTP 406 to this fetcher on two attempts; not pursued further per the two-attempts rule). location_precision set to confirmed on the strength of the contest's own arcsecond-precision coordinate plus three sources agreeing on a single, physically distinctive, named tree at a fixed park landmark (not a park-level guess). Anecdote worth leading with: a chestnut cut to a stump by shelling in WWI, that grew back as four trunks, and was then spared a second death sentence in WWII only because felling it threatened the houses below.
